title: Prices and trade-offs

screens.title: Lesson 5: Prices and trade-offs
screens.text: A price tells us what something costs, and what we give up to get it. Let us learn about prices. Press Start when you are ready.

art.alt: A price tag and a shopping cart

screens.text: At a store, things have a price tag. For example, a store might sell a snack for 4 dollars. We can pay with cash from our hand, or with a card swipe.

art.alt: A store snack that costs 4 dollars

screens.text: With cash, 4 dollars leaves our hand and the store has it.

art.alt: Cash goes from our hand to the store

screens.text: With a swipe, nothing is in our hand, but 4 dollars still leaves. The account goes from 20 dollars down to 16 dollars. A swipe is real money leaving.

art.alt: Swipe 4 dollars: the account goes from 20 dollars to 16 dollars

screens.text: In our family, we use tokens. A special treat costs 10 tokens. We earn about 10 tokens a day, so a special treat costs about one day of earning.

screens.prompt: A special treat costs 10 tokens. We earn about 10 tokens a day. How many days of earning is a special treat?

options.label: About 5 days
options.why: That is too many. One day of earning is about 10 tokens, which is the price of the treat.

options.label: About 1 day
options.why: Yes. 10 tokens a day, and the treat is 10 tokens, so it is about one day of earning.

options.label: It is free
options.why: A treat is not free. It costs 10 tokens, which we earned.

screens.text: We can only spend each token once. Say we have 10 tokens. We can get a special treat now, or save those 10 tokens toward the treasure. We cannot do both with the same tokens. Picking one and giving up the other is a trade-off.

art.alt: A treat now, or tokens saved for the treasure

screens.prompt: We have 10 tokens. A special treat costs 10 tokens. What is true?

options.label: We can get the treat, or save the tokens. Not both.
options.why: Yes. The same 10 tokens cannot go two places. What we skip is what we gave up.

options.label: We can get the treat and still save the same tokens.
options.why: Once the tokens pay for the treat, they are gone. They cannot be saved too.

options.label: Tokens never run out.
options.why: Tokens do run out. We earn about 50 tokens a week.

screens.prompt: Is a special treat worth 10 tokens to you?

options.label: Always buy every treat.
options.why: If we buy every treat, the tokens run out and the treasure gets further away.

options.label: Never get a treat.
options.why: Treats can be a fine choice. The idea is to think, not to never buy.

options.label: It depends on what else those tokens could do. Think about the trade-off.
options.why: Yes. A price is worth paying when what we get matters more to us than what we give up.

talk.q: When did we last have a special treat? Was it worth 10 tokens?
talk.note: In our family a special treat costs 10 tokens, about one day of earning. There are no family token prices for toys or games.

talk.q: When we picked one thing, what did we give up? Is that always true when we spend?
talk.note: Yes: spending on one thing means less for another. That is the trade-off.

talk.q: At a store, a swipe takes real money out of an account. How is paying with a card like paying with cash?
talk.note: In both, money leaves and the store gets it. The store prices in the lesson are examples.

talk.q: If a child pressed Ask a grown-up in this lesson, what was the question?
talk.note: Common ones: "Do we really pay for this?" (yes, even a swipe) and what other things could cost tokens (you decide; right now only special treats do).

items.prompt: Two things at a store are close in price, and one is much better made. What is a good way to choose?

options.label: Compare what you get for the price, then decide.

items.hint: Is the price the only thing to look at?
items.why: Right. When prices are close, look at what you get.
